result:
The session clock is now anchored at the start of `main`, before argument parsing, instead of on the first time-reading. `cargo test -q -p ucal --no-fail-fast` and `cargo test -q -p xtask --no-fail-fast` both pass. `xtask lint` reports 0 violations, and `--no-default-features --features u512,std` still builds.

- **Anchor at start:** `clock::anchor()` in `crates/ucal/src/clock.rs` takes the monotonic base, then reads the wall clock, and stores the session. Calling it again keeps the first anchor. `main.rs` calls it first thing and drops the result.
- **Read failure:** If the start-up read fails, the command still runs. The session stays unanchored, and `now_instant` tries again on its first reading and returns the error itself.
- **Library callers:** They have no `main`, so `now_instant` still anchors on first use for them.
- **Cost:** Every command now reads the clock once at start-up. The old code deliberately avoided that, so I replaced its comment with the new reasoning.

I split `session_now` into `anchor_in` and `now_in`, which take the session state as a parameter, so tests can use a local state instead of the process-wide one. Three new unit tests cover it:

- Anchoring twice keeps the first anchor and monotonic base, and a later reading doesn't move them.
- A reading on an unanchored session anchors it.
- Fifty consecutive readings on an anchored session never go backwards.

No test checks that `main` actually calls `anchor()`. I added a paragraph on the start-up anchor to the "One process, one clock" section of `Documentation/CLI.md`.

I didn't add a release note. 1.12.0 is already released and there is no unreleased notes file. Nothing is committed.
